name: WHW (What, How & for Whom) / Galerija Nova
overview: WHW (Što, kako i za koga) is a curatorial collective founded in Zagreb in 1999; its members are the curators Ivet Ćurlin, Ana Dević, Nataša Ilić and Sabina Sabolović and the designer and publicist Dejan Kršić (WHW).
The Zagreb team also includes the curator Ana Kovačić and Gordana Borić, who manages finances and EU projects; the office is at Bogovićeva 1 (WHW).
From 2003 to 2023 WHW ran Galerija Nova, a non-profit gallery in central Zagreb owned by the City of Zagreb (WHW).
funding_verdict: WHW / Galerija Nova: public and foundation grants: Croatian state and Zagreb city money, EU programmes and private arts foundations
wider_context: In December 2022 the City of Vienna's panel found all twenty applicants for the Kunsthalle Wien directorship wanting, including WHW, and readvertised the post (Artforum, 19 December 2022, citing Der Standard).
Kunsthalle Wien board member Boris Marte, board chair of the Erste Foundation, resigned in protest, saying the board had not been consulted (Artforum).
On 10 January 2023 the museum confederation L'Internationale published a letter calling the city's explanation inadequate and asking councillor Veronica Kaup-Hasler to reconsider (L'Internationale).
This concerns the Vienna institution three WHW members directed, not WHW's Zagreb funding; ERSTE Foundation, whose chair resigned from the Kunsthalle board, is also on WHW's own funder list.

name: Museo Provincial de Granma Manuel Muñoz Cedeño
overview: Provincial museum at Calle Francisco Maceo No. 55, between Donato del Mármol and José Joaquín Palma, in Bayamo's historic centre, which EcuRed says was declared a National Monument in 1935 and ratified in 1978.

EcuRed says it opened on 19 October 1982 as the Museo Histórico de Bayamo, with culture minister Armando Hart Dávalos, the Nicaraguan poet Ernesto Cardenal and Communist Party and government leaders of Granma present.
Named for Manuel Muñoz Cedeño, born on the site on 1 January 1813, the musician who set Pedro Figueredo's La Bayamesa for orchestra, the march that became Cuba's national anthem (EcuRed).
funding_verdict: Museo Provincial de Granma Manuel Muñoz Cedeño: state museum tied by Radio Bayamo to the Centro Provincial de Patrimonio Cultural en Granma, within the Ministry of Culture's heritage system

name: Museo Provincial Ignacio Agramonte
overview: Provincial general museum at Avenida de los Mártires No. 2, between Rotario and Ignacio Sánchez, in the La Vigía district of Camagüey (provincial culture portal).

Opened on 23 December 1955 and directed from the start by Mario Aquiles Betancourt, according to EcuRed. The opening honoured the birth of Major General Ignacio Agramonte y Loynaz, who gives the museum its name.
A private Patronato Pro Museo collected donations toward it from 1941 and resolved in a 1942 motion to keep clear of the state (EcuRed).
funding_verdict: Museo Provincial Ignacio Agramonte: state museum with its own page on Camagüey's provincial culture directorate portal, in the Ministry of Culture's heritage system

name: Teatro Tomás Terry
overview: National Monument opposite Parque Martí in the centre of Cienfuegos, at Avenida 56 and Calle 27 (EcuRed).
EcuRed dates the opening to 12 February 1890, with the opera Martha, after the first stone was laid on 19 December 1887.
Named for Tomás Terry Adán, whom EcuRed calls a slave-owning sugar planter, considered the wealthiest man on the island at the time.
funding_verdict: Teatro Tomás Terry: built in 1887 to 1890 with Terry family money; listed on Cienfuegos's culture portal, and its café is run by the state company Artex

press_items.title: Julio César Contreras, "En Cienfuegos, un Festival de Música deslucido y un reguetonero que se lleva todo el público" (2024)
Julio César Contreras, "En el café del Teatro Terry, en Cienfuegos, los negocios se hacen detrás de la barra" (2024)

name: Ballet Nacional de Cuba
overview: Classical ballet company based at the Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso (Wikipedia; its archived site).
Alicia Alonso founded it in 1948 with her husband, Fernando (New York Times). Wikipedia adds his brother Alberto, dates the founding to 28 October 1948 and names it Ballet Alicia Alonso.
The company was nationalised after the 1959 revolution (New York Times) and took the name Ballet Nacional de Cuba (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Ballet Nacional de Cuba: state-funded: the Cuban state, with a small UK charity raising money for equipment and productions
wider_context: The New York Times describes inflation, power rationing that leaves Havana without electricity for up to 10 hours a day, and the government's first request for World Food Programme aid in 2024.
A dancer who left in 2024 told the Times she left because of what was happening outside the company, not the company itself. The company is state-funded and its dancers live in that economy.

press_items.outlet: The New York Times (syndicated by The San Juan Daily Star)
press_items.title: Nina Strochlic, "For many Cuban ballet dancers, forging a path forward means leaving" (2025)

press_items.outlet: Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour
press_items.title: Associated Press, "Alicia Alonso, grande dame of Cuban ballet, dies at 98" (2019)

name: Biblioteca Nacional de Cuba José Martí
overview: National library of Cuba on Avenida 20 de Mayo in Plaza de la Revolución, Havana. It heads the national public library network, which its site puts at 387 institutions (EcuRed gives 411).
Created on 18 October 1901 by Military Order 234 of the US occupation government. Its first director, Domingo Figarola Caneda, donated its first books from his own collection (library site, EcuRed).
Named for José Martí in 1949, on Fernando Ortiz's initiative, for the building then planned (EcuRed, library site).
funding_verdict: Biblioteca Nacional José Martí: mainly public: Ministry of Culture; Spain's AECID contributed over 1 million euros to a 2012 renovation

name: Casa de las Américas
overview: Cultural institution in the Vedado district of Havana, at Calle 3ra and G (its archived site, 2023).

Created by law on 28 April 1959 and opened on 4 July 1959 in the former Casa Continental de la Cultura, an Art Deco building of the 1940s put up for the Sociedad Colombista Panamericana (EcuRed). The law's number is 229 on Spanish Wikipedia and 299 on EcuRed.

Haydée Santamaría was its first director (1959 to 1980). Mariano Rodríguez followed until 1986, Roberto Fernández Retamar led it from 1986 to 2019, and Abel Prieto has led it since late 2019 (Spanish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Casa de las Américas: mainly public: Cuban Ministry of Culture

name: Cinemateca de Cuba
overview: Film archive and screening programme of ICAIC, housed since 20 October 2020 in Alfredo Guevara's former home at Calle 11 No. 806, between 2 and 4, Vedado, Havana (EcuRed, state encyclopedia, archive copy of 12 November 2024; OnCuba).
Its own chronology and EcuRed date its creation to 6 February 1960, as a cultural department of ICAIC; OnCuba names Héctor García Mesa as founder.

Spanish Wikipedia instead says Germán Puig founded a Cinemateca de Cuba in 1951 at the FIAF congress in Cambridge, citing a 2004 paper by Emmanuel Vincenot. EcuRed says an earlier film club used the name without holding films and calls crediting it with the founding an error.
funding_verdict: Cinemateca de Cuba: state-funded: Ministry of Culture through ICAIC
wider_context: 2014: a protest statement by Cuban filmmakers said the Ministry of Culture and ICAIC, the Cinemateca's parent, forced the Havana festival to withdraw Regreso a Ítaca (OnCuba, 2015).
2016: Fernando Pérez publicly rejected ICAIC's exclusion of Santa y Andrés from the Havana festival (OnCuba, 2016).
2020: ICAIC removed Sueños al pairo from the Muestra Joven, and other young filmmakers withdrew their films in solidarity (OnCuba, 2020).

2023: the Asamblea de Cineastas Cubanos, which met at the Cine 23 y 12, the Cinemateca's usual venue, condemned the handling of the documentary La Habana de Fito and declared that Cuban cinema is not ICAIC (OnCuba, July 2023).
The Cinemateca is a department of ICAIC.

name: EGREM
overview: Cuban state record and music publishing company based in Havana, called the Empresa de Grabaciones y Ediciones Musicales. Wikipedia says it belongs to the government of Cuba, and EcuRed lists it in the Ministry of Culture's system.
Founded on 31 March 1964, after the 1960 nationalisations, in the premises and with the equipment of the Panart studio, which Wikipedia calls the first Cuban-owned private studio, founded in 1944.
Wikipedia, citing Juventud Rebelde, gives its catalogue as more than 70,000 recordings, including Benny Moré, Chucho Valdés, Silvio Rodríguez and the Buena Vista Social Club musicians.
funding_verdict: EGREM: state company: income from recordings, publishing and licensing, with Sony deals abroad

name: Estudio Figueroa-Vives
overview: Private studio-gallery in the founders' home in the Vedado neighbourhood of Havana, Calle 21 No. 303, between H and I (studio site).
Founded on 9 October 1995 by the curator Cristina Vives and the photographer José A. Figueroa. Their daughter, the curator Cristina Figueroa, also runs it (studio site, Havana Times).
The site calls it one of the first autonomous, self-financed studio-galleries of contemporary Cuban art, and a private space that has still worked with institutions, academies and artists.
funding_verdict: Estudio Figueroa-Vives: self-financed by the founding family, by its own account; the Norwegian Embassy is a named collaborator
wider_context: The same Art Newspaper article says artists and rights groups were campaigning for repeal of Decree 349, which they say further censors artistic dissent.
The connection: the article quotes the studio's director, Cristina Figueroa-Vives, on the state's role in Havana's cultural spaces.

press_items.title: IPS Cuba, "An Independent Cuban Art Gallery Reaches 25 Years" (2020)
Nicole Martinez, "Cuban galleries rebound as Havana Biennial opens" (2019)

name: Festival Internacional Jazz Plaza
overview: Annual jazz festival in Havana, first held in 1980 and organised by the Instituto Cubano de la Música (EcuRed, state encyclopedia, archive copy of 23 February 2020).
It grew out of jam sessions at the Casa de la Cultura of the Plaza municipality organised by the musician Bobby Carcassés, whom an EFE text carried by 14ymedio in 2024 calls its founding father.

Víctor Rodríguez is president of the festival, Roberto Fonseca its artistic director and Indira Fajardo president of the Instituto Cubano de la Música (Prensa Latina, a state agency; festival press note for the 41st edition).
funding_verdict: Festival Internacional Jazz Plaza: mainly public: Ministry of Culture through the Instituto Cubano de la Música

press_items.title: José Lassa, "Termina el Festival Jazz Plaza y la noche habanera vuelve a quedar en silencio" (2025)

name: Fototeca de Cuba
overview: Photo archive, museum and gallery in an 18th-century two-storey building at Mercaderes 307 on Plaza Vieja in Old Havana (Cuba Business Report).
Opened on 16 November 1986 to keep, study and promote the country's photographic heritage and to show international photography (EcuRed; CNAP).

It holds the national photographic archive, transferred from the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (Cuba Business Report). English Wikipedia puts the collection at more than 700,000 photographs; EcuRed says the collection is being digitised and catalogued.
funding_verdict: Fototeca de Cuba: mainly public: Ministry of Culture through CNAP

name: Instituto de Artivismo Hannah Arendt (INSTAR)
overview: Independent art and civic-education institute at Tejadillo 214, Old Havana, in the home of its founder, the artist Tania Bruguera (14ymedio, 2015; INSTAR site).
Founded in 2015. Its first act was a 100-hour public reading of Hannah Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism at the address, during the 12th Havana Biennial (INSTAR).
Named for Arendt, whose work INSTAR says was left out of Cuban school curricula.
funding_verdict: INSTAR: self-funded: its founder's studio and a crowdfunding campaign, with documenta fifteen support in 2022 from three foundations, Lumbung and merchandise sales
wider_context: The Cuban state, which does not fund INSTAR, has acted against Bruguera and the institute. Hyperallergic (7 January 2015) reported her arrests on 30 December 2014, on 31 December and, on her sister's account, on 1 January 2015, over a planned open-microphone performance in Revolution Square, and her release on 2 January with her passport confiscated. INSTAR says more than 83 people were detained and charges were dropped after nine months; documenta says she has been repeatedly imprisoned and placed under house arrest.

Unverified: TV presenter Humberto López accused Bruguera, the 27N group and other activists of US government ties and US financing, from 14ymedio's report of 3 June 2021 on a group confronting Bruguera at INSTAR's door. INSTAR's reports name its income sources as the Kickstarter campaign, Estudio Bruguera and, in 2022, the documenta fifteen support listed above.

Roger Berkowitz of Bard's Hannah Arendt Center, who took part in INSTAR's final installation at documenta fifteen, wrote on 25 September 2022 that the exhibition was marred by charges of antisemitism returned with accusations of racism. documenta counted INSTAR in its lumbung network by 29 March 2021.

press_items.title: staff report (no byline shown), "Tania Bruguera's Tribute to Hannah Arendt Worries Cuban State Security" (2015)
Laurie Rojas, "Después de Fidel: dissident art in Cuba flourishes after Castro's death" (2018)
Valentina Di Liscia, "Artist Tania Bruguera Detained in Havana For the Third Time in a Week" (2020)

name: Museo Ernest Hemingway (Finca Vigía)
overview: House museum at Finca Vigía in San Francisco de Paula, about 15 kilometres from central Havana (EcuRed, OnCuba).
Hemingway bought the house in December 1940 and lived there until 1960. The Catalan architect Miguel Pascual y Baguer built it in 1886 (Wikipedia, EcuRed).
EcuRed states that Hemingway's widow, Mary Welsh, gave the property to the Cuban state in August 1961 after meeting Fidel Castro, and that it became a museum on 21 July 1962.
funding_verdict: Museo Ernest Hemingway (Finca Vigía): state-run through the CNPC, with conservation paid by US donors through the Finca Vigía Foundation

name: Museo Nacional de Artes Decorativas
overview: Decorative arts museum in a mansion at Calle 17 No. 502, between D and E, in the Vedado (EcuRed; English Wikipedia).
Opened on 24 July 1964 (EcuRed; Spanish Wikipedia).
Building: designed in Paris by the architects P. Virad and M. Destuque and built between 1924 and 1927 (English Wikipedia; CubaPLUS spells the second name Dastugue).
funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de Artes Decorativas: mainly public: Ministry of Culture through the National Council of Cultural Heritage (CNPC)

name: Museo Nacional de Historia Natural de Cuba
overview: National natural history museum at Calle Obispo 61, corner of Oficios, on the Plaza de Armas in Old Havana (museum site). English Wikipedia says the building is a former United States embassy.

The museum's own history dates it to a 1959 project, the Museo Cubano de Ciencias Naturales. The project became the Museo de Ciencias "Felipe Poey" in 1962 to 1963, and in the stage from 1964 to 1980 its exhibitions opened to the public for the first time.

A restructuring from 1985 to 1991 turned it into the Museo Nacional de Historia Natural. The Capitolio was chosen as its home among the sites considered, and the history page marks a "new seat" stage from 1992 (museum site).
funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de Historia Natural: mainly public: Ministry of Science, Technology and Environment (CITMA)

name: Museo Nacional de la Música
overview: Museum of Cuban musical history and instruments in the Casa Pons, Calle Capdevila 1 between Habana and Aguiar, at the entrance to Old Havana (EcuRed; Spanish Wikipedia; Prensa Latina, 2024).

EcuRed dates its inauguration to 9 September 1971; the first donation that year, two guitars and decorations of the troubadour María Teresa Vera, went to the Sala de las Mamparas of the Museo Colonial (EcuRed).
Diario de Cuba gives its first name as the Museo y Archivo de la Música Cubana, renamed Museo Nacional de la Música from 1976.
funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de la Música: mainly public: the Cuban Music Institute of the Ministry of Culture, with donated collections

name: Museo de Arte Colonial
overview: Museum of colonial furniture and decorative art in the house facing the Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana, which the Historian's Office calls the oldest building around the square (Historian's Office, archive copy of 28 June 2017; Spanish Wikipedia).

Building: a house of 1720 built for Luis Chacón, then governor of Cuba; it takes the name Casa Bayona from his grandson José de Bayona y Chacón, first Count of Casa Bayona (Spanish Wikipedia; OnCuba).

From 1856 the house held the Real Colegio de Escribanos, the newspaper La Discusión and the Arechabala liquor firm; the National Commission of Museums and Monuments restored it in 1963 (Historian's Office).
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte Colonial: mainly public: Office of the City Historian, on the state budget, ticket and shop income and authorised donations
wider_context: GAESA, the armed forces' business group, runs hotels, the Mariel port and the Banco Financiero Internacional (AP, 2016). The US State Department's Cuba Restricted List of November 2017 names GAESA, Compañía Turística Habaguanex S.A. and Habaguanex hotels in Old Havana (Federal Register 2017-24449).
The connection: Habaguanex was the Historian's Office's business arm until GAESA took it over in 2016; the museum's entry fees and shop income stayed with the Office (AP).

name: Taller Experimental de Gráfica de La Habana
overview: Printmaking workshop and gallery in a former warehouse at Callejón del Chorro 62, beside the Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana (OnCuba, 2022).
Founded on 30 July 1962 in a small space on the Plaza de la Catedral that shared a portico with the Palacio del Conde de Lombillo; the muralist Orlando Suárez was its first director (OnCuba).

EcuRed names the Chilean painter José Venturelli with Suárez as the main movers behind it, nicknamed the Taller de la Plaza; Prensa Latina (2025) names Suárez and José A. Díaz Peláez as founding artists.
funding_verdict: Taller Experimental de Gráfica: earned income from print sales, courses and commissions; founded by the Cuban state and listed in 2013 by CNAP, a Ministry of Culture body

name: Teatro Nacional de Cuba
overview: Theatre complex on the Plaza de la Revolución at Paseo and 39, Vedado, Havana (EcuRed).
President Carlos Prío Socarrás approved the site in February 1951, and architect Julio Conesa won the design competition held that year (EcuRed; Havana Times, 2012).
After his coup of March 1952 Fulgencio Batista laid the first stone at a public ceremony; EcuRed dates it to 29 June 1952.
funding_verdict: Teatro Nacional de Cuba: state-funded: the Ministry of Culture through the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas
